newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish business leader Svanholm dies, aged 62.
newsitem.headline: Swedish business leader Svanholm dies, aged 62.

text.p: Bert-Olof Svanholm, a leading Swedish businessman who had been chairman of AB Volvo since 1994, died Tuesday at age 62, his family said.

Svanholm, a former head of international engineering giant ABB AB who was also chairman of the Confederation of Swedish Industries, had been ill for several years and his health had deteriorated in recent weeks. His family declined to disclose the nature of his illness.
His death prompted a flow of tributes from the country's top politicians and business figures.
"Swedish business has lost a skilful and respected leader," Prime Minister Goran Persson said in a statement.
Svanholm, who was born in Nordmaling in northern Sweden, was educated at the Royal Institute of Technology, Sweden's top engineering university.
He started his career at construction company Nya Asfalt AB (now part of NCC AB) in 1961, moving to chemical group KemaNOrd AB in 1969 and then becoming a division head at Nitro Nobel in 1973.
In 1978 he took over the helm at Nitro Nobel as managing director.

After a spell at Swedish Match, Svanholm jointed Asea AB as as managing director and oversaw the 1988 merger of that company with Brown Boveri Ltd, which created ABB, an international engineering giant. He headed ABB until 1996.

"Sweden's business sector has lost an outstanding leader," Percy Barnevik, the current chairman of ABB, said in a statement. "He cleverly managed to combine commerical company leadership with a deep insight into how one could improve an organisation through developing and investing in individuals in an organisation."
"His long industrial experience has been invaluable to Volvo," it said in a statement. "We deeply regret his death, which also means the loss of a strong figure in Swedish business."

In recent weeks Svanholm had headed a group of more than 100 business leaders in a battle against the current Swedish government, saying its economic policies and agreement to phase out Sweden's nuclear power industry was hurting the business community.
"He was the most forceful person I have ever known -- very strong in everything that he did," a colleague told Reuters.
"He had a strong commitment to the industrial world and was very interested in education in every way that could help develop people and companies."
Svanholm was the chairman of the Royal Academy of Engineering in Stockholm at the time of his death. He was also chairman of the Chalmers Technical High School in Gothenburg, southern Sweden.
He is survived by his wife, Laila, and two adult sons.
